Cathode import premiums have edged up slightly over the past two weeks, and according to market insiders are now in the range of $70-80/t. However, we have also heard of some deals being settled as low as $60/t for lower quality material. EW premiums have remained relatively flat following a slight contraction in late June, and are now being quoted at around the US$50/t mark. Overall, market insiders have reported that demand has been flat, and sentiment remains predominantly bearish despite some slight hope for an H2 revival. The fall in demand from May to June has continued into July, with the seasonal uptick in demand failing to materialise. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** **July 2012** www.crugroup.com Furthermore, the negative SHFE /LME arbitrage has re-intensified as LME prices have moved up ahead of SHFE prices, thus dampening demand for imported material. After a slight decline in the Shanghai bonded warehouse stocks to around 500,000t in the second half of June, bonded stocks rose slightly in mid-July to approximately 550,000t according to market participants. Preliminary customs data for copper trade indicates that total imports of anode, refined metal and copper semis into China fell to 346,223t in June, down by 17.5% from the prior month. Arrivals of refined metal amounted to approximately 250,000t, down by 17.2% m-o-m. This supports our expectation from the last issue of this report that weak fundamentals, a negative arbitrage and a decline in the use of copper as collateral would limit imports. We expect June exports of refined copper to have fallen sharply from the record export level witnessed in May, when shipments reached 102,375t of cathode. Much of the export activity during May and early June was attributed to Chinese smelters covering short positions on the LME, with the material shipped to Asian LME warehouses. Looking ahead, market insiders’ opinions are somewhat divided. Some foresee copper demand improving in the remainder of the year, supported by the government’s announcement that it may double railway investment in H2. Of the RMB448B (US$70B) railway budget, approximately RMB300B (US$47B) has yet to be spent this year. Furthermore, the positive effects of this year’s monetary loosening and the various subs

idies introduced in H1 are also expected to materialise before the year end.  Refined copper production increased by 7.0% m-o-m in June to 518,000t, indicating that smelters in particular are optimistic on refined copper demand in H2. 

In contrast, many market insiders point to a 6.9% y-o-y fall in foreign direct investment as a sign of times to come.  Many believe that, thus far, the government’s economic stimuli have been too feeble to offset the economy’s poor momentum.  Certainly, a number of market participants we spoke with stated that they are hoping for further announcements of monetary loosening or pro-construction policies which would support copper demand.  Furthermore, fabricators are exercising a very cautious buying strategy, keeping cathode inventories low by operating on a hand-to-mouth basis in the light of an uncertain demand outlook and tight credit.  Lastly, any potential boost to future demand will also be offset by high end-use inventory levels, which need to be worked down before copper consumption benefits. 

# Markets for smelters’ raw materials remain tight 

We have heard that spot terms for clean concentrate between merchants and smelters have remained tight at around the $40/4.0¢ mark, with many participants reporting to us that the terms are in the range of $35-40/3.54.0¢.  However, others hold the view that $40/4.0¢ is the lower limit at present, and we hear that in the last fortnight the China Smelter Purchasing Team (CSPT) has called for a minimum of $50/5.0¢ for imported clean concentrates.  However, any upward pressure is constrained by the recent ramp-up of operations at PASAR’s Leyte smelter in the Philippines following a January fire.  The end of maintenance downtime at Jinlong and the start-up of Yunnan Tin’s new smelter will also keep the concentrate market tight, although we have heard that the latter is currently experiencing difficulties ramping up. 

The No.  2 scrap market, meanwhile, has also remained tight as merchants continue to withhold material as a result of low refined copper prices.  In addition, the negative arbitrage between the SHFE and the LME is

restricting imports and poorer than expected scrap generation is constraining supply.  Furthermore, 50,000t/y of capacity has been added at China’s Lihua International secondary smelter, which is set to boost scrap demand. Spot discounts for No.2 scrap in mid-July have hovered around the US$425/t for imported material, and around US$480/t for domestic material. 

# Details of Chinese smelter shutdowns released 

In mid-July, China’s MIIT issued the list of the Chinese smelters using outdated capacity that are to be closed during 2012.  It was announced in April that nearly 700,000t of copper production capacity is to be closed.  An analysis of the list reinforces our original opinion that it will have only a limited impact on refined copper producti

on and smelters’ concentrate requirements.  However, a significant amount of the capacity does use scrap, either in copper cathode, copper anode or semis products, so the closures will help to relieve the pressure on scrap supply. 

The list includes 43 operations with a total capacity of 714,200t/y copper, most of which are only small and operating at a low rate of capacity utilisation.  Of the total, 50,000t/y is accounted for by capacity that is being, or has recently been, replaced with significantly larger capacity.  These operations are:  Baotou Huading in Inner Mongolia, where the 30,000t/y to be closed will be replaced by 70,000t/y later in 2012; Fushun Hongtoushan in Liaoning where new capacity was added in 2010 and Chifeng Fubang where 5,000t/y is to be closed, but 100,000t/y of new capacity was brought on stream in 2011. 

The most significant closures will be 60,000t/y at Chifeng Yunnan Copper’s Jinfeng smelter, 30,000t/y at Henan Jinpeng Copper Co.’s secondary smelter and 25,000t/y at Kunming Jinshui Copper Smelting Co.’s smelter.  At Jinfeng, capacity was expanded from 60,000t/y to 120,000t/y in 2009, and it is the original capacity that is to close.  The plant will continue to operate.  We assume that the same level of refined production will be maintained and the company will source third party blister or scrap in addition to its own blister production.  However, concentrate requirements will fall. 

Of the remainder, we estimate that more than 250,000t/y is accounted for by semis producers, mostly using secondary materials, with the balance being secondary smelters. 

Further to the above announcements of shutdowns to outdated smelting capacity, the Chinese government has taken a more stern approach to approving new smelting projects.  Earlier this month, the construction of Sichuan Hongda’s 400,000t/y smelter and refinery project was cancelled by the local government after local residents protested due to their concerns over the potential environmental impact, in spite of the project having received environmental approval in March 2012.  Earlier in the year, under similar circumstances, approvals of environmental impact assessments were suspended for Guangxi Nanguo Copper’s 150,000t/y copper smelting project and Qinghai Copper’s 100,000t/y copper smelting project by the Ministry of Environmental Protection (MEP).  These developments are significant in that they are the first instances where the construction of a new, technologically advanced and efficient copper plants have been halted due to local opposition.  Community action is often a major disruptive factor in other parts of the world, notably Peru and Ecuador, but this is a new development in China.  Considering the country’s huge and expanding smelting/refining sector, further activism in this area could have a substantial impact on the copper market balance.

Over the last fortnight, the copper price was influenced predominantly by developments in China, rather than in the Eurozone as has frequently been the case in recent months. Prices were off to a poor start in the last fortnight, with news of a 17.5% m-o-m fall in June imports of copper to China causing the SHFE cash-month price to fall by 1.0% on Monday, 9th July, to RMB55,540/t. Subsequently, anxiety ahead of the release of Q2 GDP data for China prompted investors to exercise caution, causing the copper price to remain flat until Friday. Sentiment improved, however, on news that China’s Q2 GDP growth was the slowest in three years, as investors stirred up expectations of an imminent announcement of an economic stimulus package. This caused the SHFE cash-month price to rebound from Friday, 13th July with a peak of RMB56,150/t on Monday, 16th July. Meanwhile, the news caused the cash price on the LME to rise sharply on Friday, 13th July, before contracting on Monday, 16th July, after a lack of expected stimuli announcements in the US aggravated sentiment. On Friday, 20th July, the SHFE cash-month price closed at RMB56,000/t, supported by continuing optimism on the stimulus package. Having caught up with the LME cash price in June, the SHFE cash-month price once again fell below the LME from the beginning of July. Between 9th and 19th July, the SHFE cash-month price was, on average, US$129/t lower than the LME cash price. The arbitrage intensified to US$-155 in the week beginning 16th July. Meanwhile, the backwardation between the SHFE cash-month price and the SHFE 3-month price narrowed to an average of US$-20/t in the last fortnight. In fact, the price differential slipped into contango on several occasions, highlighting the high refined copper stock levels in China at the moment. The cathode inventory in SHFE warehouses totalled 160,973t on 20th July, up by 5,736t up on the level on 6th July. With weak demand persisting and high cathode inventories, we expect SHFE cash-month prices to remain in the RMB55,000-56,500/t range, although any significant announcements of government stimuli may see

the price being pushed towards the upper boundary.
